# Kth Largest in a Stream — Explained, One Approach at a Time

<!-- Generated by scripts/gen-explained.mjs from src/data/problems/heaps/kth-largest-stream.ts.
     Edit the data, then run `npm run docs:explained`. Edits here are overwritten. -->

**Heaps** · easy · [the same question on LeetCode](https://leetcode.com/problems/kth-largest-element-in-a-stream/)

Design a class initialized with k and a list of numbers. Each call to add(x) inserts x and returns the kth largest value seen so far.

## What the input promises

- 1 <= k <= 10^4
- 0 <= nums.length <= 10^4
- -10^4 <= nums[i], val <= 10^4
- at least k values exist when kth-largest is asked for

## Examples

| Input | Output | Why |
|---|---|---|
| `k = 3, start = [4, 5, 8, 2]; add(3) → 4; add(5) → 5; add(10) → 5` | `see calls` | After add(10) the three largest are 10, 8, 5. |

<details>
<summary>Hints, one nudge at a time — open them in order</summary>

1. You never care about anything smaller than the current kth largest.
2. Keep only the k largest values. Which structure evicts its smallest in O(log k)?
3. A min-heap of size k: its root IS the kth largest.

</details>

---

## 1. Sort per add

Keep a list, re-sort on every add, index the kth from the end. Each add costs n log n — painful for a hot path the heap serves in log k.

```python
class KthLargest:
    def __init__(self, k: int, nums: list[int]):
        self.k = k
        self.nums = list(nums)

    def add(self, x: int) -> int:
        self.nums.append(x)
        self.nums.sort()
        return self.nums[-self.k]
```

**O(n log n) per add time · O(n) space**
<details>
<summary>The same rung in Java</summary>

```java
public class KthLargest {
    private int k;
    private List<Integer> nums;

    public KthLargest(int k, int[] nums) {
        this.k = k;
        this.nums = new ArrayList<>();
        for (int num : nums) this.nums.add(num);
    }

    public int add(int x) {
        nums.add(x);
        Collections.sort(nums);
        return nums.get(nums.size() - k);
    }
}
```

</details>
<details>
<summary>The same rung in C++</summary>

```cpp
class KthLargest {
public:
    int k;
    vector<int> nums;

    KthLargest(int k, const vector<int>& nums): k(k), nums(nums) {}

    int add(int x) {
        nums.push_back(x);
        sort(nums.begin(), nums.end());
        return nums[nums.size() - k];
    }
};
```

</details>

## 2. Sorted insert (bisect)

> **Why now.** Re-sorting on every add redoes work that was already in order. Inserting into a sorted list keeps the order for the price of shifting elements.

Keep the list sorted and insert with bisect. Insertion is O(n) due to shifting, but far better constants than re-sorting; still loses to the heap asymptotically.

```python
import bisect

class KthLargest:
    def __init__(self, k: int, nums: list[int]):
        self.k = k
        self.nums = sorted(nums)

    def add(self, x: int) -> int:
        bisect.insort(self.nums, x)
        return self.nums[-self.k]
```

**O(n) per add time · O(n) space**
<details>
<summary>The same rung in Java</summary>

```java
public class KthLargest {
    private int k;
    private List<Integer> nums;

    public KthLargest(int k, int[] nums) {
        this.k = k;
        this.nums = new ArrayList<>();
        for (int num : nums) this.nums.add(num);
        Collections.sort(this.nums);
    }

    public int add(int x) {
        int idx = Collections.binarySearch(nums, x);
        if (idx < 0) idx = -idx - 1;
        nums.add(idx, x);
        return nums.get(nums.size() - k);
    }
}
```

</details>
<details>
<summary>The same rung in C++</summary>

```cpp
class KthLargest {
public:
    int k;
    vector<int> nums;

    KthLargest(int k, vector<int> nums): k(k), nums(nums) {
        sort(this->nums.begin(), this->nums.end());
    }

    int add(int x) {
        auto it = lower_bound(nums.begin(), nums.end(), x);
        nums.insert(it, x);
        return nums[nums.size() - k];
    }
};
```

</details>

## 3. The one to remember

> **Why now.** Shifting is still linear per add, and nothing here needs the full order - only the kth value. A min-heap of size k keeps that value at the root and costs a logarithm per add.

Maintain a min-heap holding exactly the k largest values seen. On add, push the new value; if the heap grows past k, pop the minimum (which by definition is no longer in the top k). The root is then the kth largest at all times. Keeping the heap small (k, not n) is the entire point.

```python
import heapq

class KthLargest:
    def __init__(self, k: int, nums: list[int]):
        self.k = k
        self.heap = nums
        heapq.heapify(self.heap)
        while len(self.heap) > k:
            heapq.heappop(self.heap)

    def add(self, x: int) -> int:
        heapq.heappush(self.heap, x)
        if len(self.heap) > self.k:
            heapq.heappop(self.heap)
        return self.heap[0]
```

**O(log k) per add time · O(k) space**
<details>
<summary>The same rung in Java</summary>

```java
public class KthLargest {
    private int k;
    private PriorityQueue<Integer> heap;

    public KthLargest(int k, int[] nums) {
        this.k = k;
        this.heap = new PriorityQueue<>();
        for (int num : nums) heap.add(num);
        while (heap.size() > k) heap.poll();
    }

    public int add(int x) {
        heap.offer(x);
        if (heap.size() > k) heap.poll();
        return heap.peek();
    }
}
```

</details>
<details>
<summary>The same rung in C++</summary>

```cpp
class KthLargest {
public:
    int k;
    priority_queue<int, vector<int>, greater<int>> heap;

    KthLargest(int k, const vector<int>& nums): k(k), heap(greater<int>()) {
        for (int num : nums) heap.push(num);
        while ((int)heap.size() > k) heap.pop();
    }

    int add(int x) {
        heap.push(x);
        if ((int)heap.size() > k) heap.pop();
        return heap.top();
    }
};
```

</details>

## The arc

| # | Approach | Cost | What it adds |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Sort per add | O(n log n) per add time · O(n) space | the baseline — nothing before it |
| 2 | Sorted insert (bisect) | O(n) per add time · O(n) space | Re-sorting on every add redoes work that was already in order. Inserting into a sorted list keeps the order for the price of shifting elements. |
| 3 | The one to remember | O(log k) per add time · O(k) space | Shifting is still linear per add, and nothing here needs the full order - only the kth value. A min-heap of size k keeps that value at the root and costs a logarithm per add. |

## Full runnable script

Every rung in one file, printed against the inputs `npm run verify:run`
drives the Java and C++ blocks with. Run it: `python explained.py`.

```python
class KthLargest_sort_per_add:
    def __init__(self, k: int, nums: list[int]):
        self.k = k
        self.nums = list(nums)

    def add(self, x: int) -> int:
        self.nums.append(x)
        self.nums.sort()
        return self.nums[-self.k]


import bisect

class KthLargest_sorted_insert_bisect:
    def __init__(self, k: int, nums: list[int]):
        self.k = k
        self.nums = sorted(nums)

    def add(self, x: int) -> int:
        bisect.insort(self.nums, x)
        return self.nums[-self.k]


import heapq

class KthLargest_the_one_to_remember:
    def __init__(self, k: int, nums: list[int]):
        self.k = k
        self.heap = nums
        heapq.heapify(self.heap)
        while len(self.heap) > k:
            heapq.heappop(self.heap)

    def add(self, x: int) -> int:
        heapq.heappush(self.heap, x)
        if len(self.heap) > self.k:
            heapq.heappop(self.heap)
        return self.heap[0]

APPROACHES = [
    KthLargest_sort_per_add,
    KthLargest_sorted_insert_bisect,
    KthLargest_the_one_to_remember,
]

# the same inputs npm run verify:run drives the Java and C++ blocks with:
# the heap being trimmed to k and staying there — [4,5,8,2] with k=3 must drop the 2 in the CONSTRUCTOR, and k=1 on an empty start has nothing to trim until the first add
CASES = [
    lambda: (3, [4,5,8,2], [3,5,10,9,4]),
    lambda: (1, [], [-3,-2,-4,0,4]),
    lambda: (2, [0], [-1,1,-2,-4,3]),
    lambda: (4, [7,7,7,7,8,3], [2,10,9,9]),
]

if __name__ == "__main__":
    for cls in APPROACHES:
        answers = []
        for make in CASES:
            *ctor, stream = make()  # constructor args, then the calls
            try:
                obj = cls(*ctor)
                answers.append([obj.add(x) for x in stream])
            except BaseException as exc:  # a rung that raises names itself
                answers.append(f"!{exc}")
        print(f"{cls.__name__:<33} -> {answers}")
```
